1394.title: Moon sighting debates
1394.hook: calculation or sighting, local or global, still debated
1394.tomorrow: Prayer times in the far north
1394.howItsDone: Muslim communities decide the start of Ramadan and the Eids in different ways: some wait for a local sighting of the crescent, some accept a sighting from another country, and some follow astronomical calculation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: social media and the tongue. Your line was the tongue has thumbs. Today, the moon.

It's the twenty-ninth night of Ramadan, and the family group chat is busy. One mosque has announced: Eid is tomorrow. Another, across town, says: not yet, we fast one more day. An aunt forwards a sighting from another country. A cousin posts an astronomy chart. Somebody asks, half joking, whether the family is allowed two Eids. Nobody is being careless. Every one of them is trying to start the feast on the right day.
screen: `TWO MOSQUES, TWO ANSWERS.` → `A SIGHTING FROM ABROAD.` → `EVERYONE WANTS THE RIGHT DAY.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Qur'an. People asked the Prophet about the new moons, and the answer, in Pickthall's translation, is: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage." The moon is the calendar, but the verse doesn't say how to read it. That comes from the hadith. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: fast when you see it, end the fast when you see it, and if it is hidden from you, complete thirty days. In another report he says his community does not write or calculate, and the month is sometimes this long and sometimes that, shown with his hands. Here's the first debate. Some scholars read these words as a command: the month begins with a human eye seeing the crescent. Others read the mention of not calculating as a description of that time, and accept astronomical calculation now that it can be done. The second debate has a story. Imam Muslim records that a man named Kurayb was in Syria at the start of Ramadan, where they saw the new moon on Friday night. Back in Medina he told Ibn 'Abbas, who said: we saw it on Saturday night, and we'll keep fasting until we complete thirty or see it ourselves. Isn't the sighting in Syria enough? Kurayb asked. No, said Ibn 'Abbas; this is how the Messenger of Allah commanded us. So some communities follow a local sighting. Others accept a sighting from anywhere, so one sighting starts the month for everyone. Others follow calculation. Each can point to something in the sources. None of them is ignoring the moon.
screen: `THE NEW MOONS: FIXED SEASONS.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `SIGHTING OR CALCULATION?` · `KURAYB: SYRIA SAW IT FIRST.` · then, large: `LOCAL OR GLOBAL?`

segments.voice: Picture a thin crescent low over the horizon just after sunset, and the people looking for it: someone on a rooftop, someone with a telescope, someone reading a table of numbers, someone waiting for a call from abroad, all facing the same sky. If any of them annoys you, notice it and let it go. If you pray, remember the people who will be fasting or feasting on a different day from you.
Moon sighting debates. Seeing with the eye or calculating, one local sighting or one for everyone: questions Muslims still weigh about when a month begins. Today's word.
Your line: one moon, many views. Every one of them is looking at the same sky. Until tomorrow.

1395.title: Prayer times in the far north
1395.word: Prayer times in the far north
1395.hook: where the sun barely sets, scholars give rulings for prayer and fasting
1395.howItsDone: Muslims living far north follow rulings from scholars and local councils: some pray and fast by the times of the nearest place with a clear day and night, some by the times of Mecca, and some by their own sky when the signs can still be seen.

segments.voice: Yesterday: moon sighting debates, and Kurayb coming home from Syria. Your line was one moon, many views. Today, the sun gets difficult too.

Midsummer, somewhere far north. It's late in the evening and the sky is still bright. A family has been fasting since before dawn, and dawn came early, because night never quite arrived. The table is set. The dates are out. Someone keeps checking the window. The sun touches the horizon, slides along it, and seems unwilling to go. When the Qur'an says fast until night, and the night barely comes, what do you do?
screen: `A TABLE SET, A SKY STILL BRIGHT.` → `THE SUN WON'T GO.` → `WHEN NIGHT BARELY COMES.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an ties the fast to the sky. In Pickthall's translation, the believers may "eat and drink until the white thread becometh distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall." Dawn and nightfall. The daily prayers are tied to the sun's movements the same way. In Mecca and Medina, the sun keeps steady hours. Far north, in summer, the dawn light may never fully fade, and in winter the day may hardly come. Scholars turn to a report in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoke of a time to come when a day would be as long as a year. His companions asked the obvious question: will one day's prayers be enough for that day? He said no; estimate its measure, and pray accordingly. So the principle is already there: when the sun stops being a usable clock, you measure. How to measure is where the views differ. Some scholars say to follow the times of the nearest place where day and night are still clearly distinct. Some say to follow the times of Mecca. Some say that if the long fast can be kept, keep it by your own sky, and estimate only when the signs disappear or the strain becomes too great. Behind all of them stands a line from the close of the same chapter, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The family at the window isn't facing a gap in their religion. They're standing where a question was already asked and answered.
screen: `DAWN AND NIGHTFALL SET THE FAST.` · `A DAY AS LONG AS A YEAR.` · `ESTIMATE ITS MEASURE.` · `NEAREST PLACE, MECCA, OR YOUR OWN SKY.` · then, large: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Picture that kitchen far north, light still at the window late at night, the table waiting, and then someone there on a winter morning, praying in the dark before a sun that will barely rise. Hold them both for a few breaths, under a sky that won't cooperate. If you pray, keep them in your prayers; if you don't, let your own sky feel a little more ordinary, and a little more of a gift.
Prayer times in the far north. Where the sun barely sets or barely rises, scholars estimate the times for prayer and fasting. Today's word.

1396.title: Refugees and the Hijra
1396.hook: the Prophet's own leaving of home, and the people on the roads today
1396.howItsDone: Some Muslim charities and mosques support refugees, and some teachers point to the Hijra and to the Ansar of Medina, who took the migrants into their homes, when they speak about welcoming people who have fled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: prayer times in the far north, a family waiting for a sunset that wouldn't come. Your line was ramadan under the midnight sun. Today, a different kind of leaving.

Two men in a cave, with the people hunting them somewhere outside. Outside is the city they grew up in, and it no longer wants them. One of them is afraid. The other says, in Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." The two are the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his friend Abu Bakr, and the journey is the Hijra, the leaving of Mecca for Medina. A story of the past, and of the people on the roads right now.
screen: `TWO MEN IN A CAVE.` → `GRIEVE NOT.` → `THE HIJRA: LEAVING HOME.`

segments.voice: Hijra is the Arabic word for this leaving. It was not a holiday. The Qur'an, in the chapter called Exile, speaks of the migrants as poor, driven out from their homes and their belongings. Tradition says the Muslim calendar counts its years from this leaving. Now look at who met them. The people of Medina, the Ansar, the helpers, took the newcomers into their homes, and the next verse of that chapter praises them. In Pickthall's words, they "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot." Fugitives is Pickthall's word for the migrants. Al-Bukhari keeps a scene from those days. One of the helpers, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', was paired as a brother with one of the newcomers, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and offered him half of everything he owned. 'Abd al-Rahman thanked him and said, in paraphrase: just show me the way to the market. A welcome on one side. Dignity on the other. The Qur'an also speaks of someone outside the faith who asks for protection. Surah nine says that if one of the idolaters seeks protection, he is to be protected and then escorted somewhere safe. So when Muslims today look at families crossing borders with what they can carry, some see the Hijra again: a Prophet who was himself once a refugee, and a city that made room. The mirror works both ways. It asks what it is to flee, and what it is to be the Ansar.
screen: `HIJRA: LEAVING A PLACE.` · `THE ANSAR MADE ROOM.` · `SHOW ME THE WAY TO THE MARKET.` · `PROTECT THE ONE WHO ASKS.` · then, large: `THEY PREFER THE FUGITIVES ABOVE THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you left somewhere, a home, a school, a country, a job: what did you carry, and who met you on the other side, or didn't? Then think of someone, anywhere, who left home this year with no choice and arrived with very little, and hold them for a while; you don't need a name. If you pray, remember them in your prayers; if you don't, simply keep them in mind.

1397.title: Poverty and zakat today
1397.hook: a blanket, a bowl and an axe: giving that lifts
1397.howItsDone: Muslims who have enough wealth calculate their zakat each year and give it through mosques, zakat funds, charities or directly to people in need who fall within the Qur'an's categories.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hijra today, a cave, a welcome in Medina, a man asking the way to the market. Your line was the hijra today. Today, what giving is for.

A man comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking for help. Is there nothing in your house? the Prophet asks. There is: a blanket, and a bowl for drinking water. The Prophet sells them to people nearby and gives the man the money: buy food for your family with part, and with the rest, an axe head, and bring it to me. He fixes a handle to it himself and sends the man out to gather wood to sell. The story is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud.
screen: `A BLANKET AND A BOWL.` → `AN AXE HEAD, A HANDLE.` → `SENT OUT TO GATHER WOOD.`

segments.voice: Zakat, the obligatory alms, is counted among the pillars of Islam: a share of wealth, given by those who have enough, to those the Qur'an names. The list is in surah nine. In Pickthall's translation it begins: "The alms are only for the poor and the needy," and goes on to name those who collect the alms, those whose hearts are to be won, captives to be freed, people in debt, the cause of Allah, and the traveler. Notice how many are about getting someone out of something: out of chains, out of debt, out of being stranded. A few verses on, the Qur'an tells the Prophet: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Purify and grow. In al-Bukhari, when the Prophet sends Mu'adh to Yemen, he tells him to teach the people that zakat is taken from their rich and returned to their poor, in the same place. And today? It is still calculated on savings, gold and business stock, and given through mosques, through charities and by hand. Some zakat funds pay off debts, or pay for a sick person's care, or help a family start a small trade. Scholars discuss which uses fit the categories in the verse, and some debate whether zakat can fund long-term projects or should go straight to people. Behind the debate is the axe in the hook. The hope is more than a meal. It's the moment someone no longer needs to ask.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one gift you've given, or meant to, and picture what happened after it left your hands: did it feed someone for a day, clear a debt, buy a tool? Don't grade yourself; just ask the axe question: could a gift help someone stand up, as well as eat? If you pray, ask for a giving that purifies and grows.

1398.title: Scholarship today
1398.hook: al-Azhar, Najaf, Qom, Deoband, Medina, and online
1398.howItsDone: Muslims who want to study their tradition in depth may enroll at a university or seminary such as al-Azhar, a hawza in Najaf or Qom, a madrasa in the Deobandi tradition, or the Islamic University of Medina, or join classes with a teacher online or at a local mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday: poverty and zakat today, and an axe head with a handle the Prophet fixed himself. Your line was zakat can lift. Today, where knowledge is handed on.

A sheet of paper, handwritten, with a list of names running down it. At the bottom, a student's name. Above it, the teacher who heard the student recite and gave permission to teach. Above that, the teacher's teacher, and another, and another, climbing back through the generations. It's called an ijaza, a permission, and in the tradition it's how knowledge is handed on: not just from a book, but from a person who learned it from a person.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES, CLIMBING BACK.` → `IJAZA: A PERMISSION.` → `FROM PERSON TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an gives the student's prayer in a few words. Pickthall translates it: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." And in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise. So where are those paths today? Start in Cairo, at al-Azhar, a mosque and a university where Sunni students study Qur'an, hadith, law and Arabic. Go east to Iraq and Iran, to Najaf and Qom, cities of the hawza, the Shia seminaries, where students sit with teachers and train as scholars of law. Then Deoband, a town in northern India with a seminary whose name is carried by schools in other countries too. Then Medina, the Prophet's own city, home to the Islamic University. Each place has its own emphases, its own teachers and its own way of teaching, and Muslims hold different views about them. And then a new place: online. Recorded lessons, live classes, a teacher in one country and a student in another, sometimes still ending with an ijaza given across a screen. Some teachers warn that a video can't correct your mistakes the way a person in the room can. Others say it opens a door that was closed to people far from any city of learning. The old shape still holds: a student, a teacher, a text, and a question asked out loud.

1399.howItsDone: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an recitation, hadith and fiqh in mosques, seminaries, universities and online, and communities differ on the settings in which women teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday: scholarship today, from Cairo, Najaf and Qom to Deoband, Medina and a laptop. Your line was where they study. Today, who teaches.

A group of women in Medina has a complaint, and they bring it straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. The men, they say, are always around you. They get all your time. So give us a day of our own. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. He agrees. He promises them a day, meets them on it, and teaches them. No one in the report tells them to wait for their husbands to pass the lessons on. They asked for a teacher, and they got one.
screen: `THE MEN GET ALL YOUR TIME.` → `GIVE US A DAY.` → `HE AGREES, AND TEACHES THEM.`

segments.voice: Begin with the Qur'an, which speaks to women and men side by side. In Pickthall's translation, one verse runs: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe," and it goes on, pair after pair, the truthful, the patient, the humble, the fasting, the ones who remember Allah, and promises all of them forgiveness and a reward. Then the women who asked for a day. They didn't wait for knowledge to trickle down to them. They went to the source. Tradition says the companions brought their questions to a woman too: 'Aisha, the Prophet's wife. Al-Bukhari's collection carries her reports, and in some she corrects what others had passed on, as when she answers a report about the dead and the weeping of their families. Tradition remembers women after her too, who taught hadith and law in their own cities, and whose names stand in the chains of transmission alongside men's. One of them, Karima of Merv, is remembered for teaching Sahih al-Bukhari itself. And today? Women teach the Qur'an and its recitation, hadith, and fiqh, the law of daily life, in mosques, seminaries and colleges, in living rooms and online classes. Communities and schools of thought hold different views on how and where women should teach, and to whom, and those views are held seriously. But the line from the hook still runs: women asking for a teacher, and a Prophet who set the day.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a woman who taught you something that stuck, a mother, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt in a kitchen, a neighbor who knew things, and picture her face as she explained it. What did she know that you didn't? Thank her in your head for a moment, and if you pray, remember her in your prayers.
Women scholars today. Women teaching Qur'an, hadith and the law of daily life, in a line that runs back to 'Aisha and the women who asked for a day. Today's word.
Your line: she teaches. And she has, from Medina all the way until now. Until tomorrow.

1400.title: Art and music debates
1400.hook: scholars differ on musical instruments, while nasheed and recitation flourish
1400.howItsDone: Muslims hold different views on musical instruments: some avoid them and listen only to the voice or a frame drum, others enjoy music they consider clean in words and setting, and recitation of the Qur'an and nasheed are part of daily life for people holding either view.

segments.voice: Yesterday: women scholars today, and the women of Medina who asked for a day of their own. Your line was she teaches. Today goes deeper into day one hundred forty-eight, where scholars who differ on music first came up.

It's Eid in Medina, and in 'Aisha's house two girls are singing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down nearby, his face turned away. Then Abu Bakr walks in, 'Aisha's father, and he's shocked. Musical instruments of Satan, he says, in the house of the Messenger of Allah? The Prophet turns toward him and says, in paraphrase: leave them, Abu Bakr. Every people has its feast day, and this is ours. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aisha herself.
screen: `TWO GIRLS SINGING ON EID.` → `ABU BAKR OBJECTS.` → `LEAVE THEM. THIS IS OUR FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here is where scholars differ. Al-Bukhari also records a saying, in a chapter on drinks, that some of the Prophet's community will one day treat as lawful silk, wine and musical instruments. Some scholars read this as forbidding instruments, and allow only the voice, and perhaps a simple frame drum at weddings and on Eid. Others question how that report reaches al-Bukhari, or read it as condemning a whole scene of drinking and excess rather than the instruments alone, and allow music whose words and setting are clean. Both sides are reading the same collection carefully. Neither is careless about the faith. Now the voice. Nasheed, songs sung with the voice alone, or with a drum, are sung at weddings, in school halls and in headphones. And there is recitation of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measured cadence." Al-Bukhari keeps a report in which the Prophet hears Abu Musa reciting and tells him, in paraphrase, that he has been given a flute from among the flutes of the family of David. The praise for a beautiful voice compares it to a musical instrument. So the debate about instruments goes on, held in good faith, and the voices keep rising.
screen: `SILK, WINE AND INSTRUMENTS.` · `TWO READINGS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.` · `NASHEED: THE VOICE ALONE.` · `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAVID.` · then, large: `CHANT THE QUR'AN IN MEASURED CADENCE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose view on music differs from yours, stricter or looser, and picture them choosing as they do because they're trying to be careful with something they love; hold that for a few breaths without arguing. If you like, let a voice you love play quietly in your memory, a recitation, a lullaby, a nasheed, a song from home. If you pray, give thanks for voices.
